title: Playing schools and a Jewish old folks' home: the trombonist who changed the program
summary: The band played free at schools and homes; a trombonist always swapped his announced number, once breaking down while playing his mother's favorite hymn.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: But where did you play? At schools, at public places? There was no admission charge, I take it.
Yes. We played schools, old folks homes, settlement houses, filohouses -- yes, that's right, because they had to have music too, you know.
Yes, uh-huh. And, you know, it's a funny thing about one of the programs that I played. I'll tell you something funny. I played a Jewish old folks' home, and
I had a trombone player -- this fellow that played a trombone, and was just about tit for tat for Dorsey, man, for singing the trombone. And you know how Dorsey can make a trombone sing.
So I would like to hear him play "Russian Lullaby", because he would play it so sweetly. So -- but this fellow, he had a knack that he didn't like for you to tell him what to play.

MR. RANDOLPH: Whenever you would announce one playing, diplomatically he would show you he wanted to play something else. So this time, so -- he would do this all the time. So I told the audience, I said, ladies and gentlemen, I says, I have a young man back here on this trombone, I says, and I would like for you to hear him play "Russian Lullaby". He plays it so sweetly. I said, his name is Mr. Lawson, stand up, Mr. Lawson. And he comes up there, he says, Mr. Randolph, for these dear people, looking at these dear people out here, I would like to play for them my mother's favorite hymn. Then I says, now, ladies and gentlemen, there has been a change in the program. I says, Mr. Lawson wants to play his mother's favorite hymn. And he says, that's "Blessed Assurance." So I had a lady pianist, her name was Marcia [Florie]. So Miss [Florie] made the introduction on the piano, and he started (musical sounds) -- wait, wait, wait, I can't play it (unintelligible). So I had to go

to another number, and I told him, please excuse Mr. Lawson, he kind of got a little overcome there. And he gets to thinking about his dear old mother and playing that hymn. See, it boomeranged back and he actually was crying.

Yeah, he did, he cried, because it was his mother's favorite hymn, but he was going to get back at me and play his mother's favorite hymn, but in playing it, he began to -- I guess, think about his mother while he was playing it, and then he cries, because I think his mother had passed or something at the time. So the boys really kidded him about that. That was a funny thing. But he would always do that. And if I would say -- if I'd ask him to play any sweet number, he'd change it.

One time, I called a number that I wanted him to play and he changed it to a Indian Love Call. And he forgot the Indian Love Call, so the boys said he had all the little braves coming out, Big Chief, Sitting Bull and all of them. They really kidded him, so -- but he never did stop changing those numbers.
